title: Assessing Plastic Impacts in Life Cycle Assessment: A Practitioner’s Guide
Assessing Plastic Impacts in Life Cycle Assessment: A Practitioner’s Guide
text:
Objective
The objective of this methodological guide is to provide LCA practitioners with a detailed understanding of how to apply CFs for the assessment of potential biodiversity impacts associated with plastic emissions. The guide provides step-by-step support for practitioners seeking to implement the physical effects on biota CFs in their assessments, from the identification and preparation of relevant inventory flows to the calculation and interpretation of midpoint and damage results.
These CFs were developed within the MarILCA framework. The MarILCA working group was created in 2018 with the support of the Life Cycle Initiative of UN Environment and the Forum for Sustainability through Life Cycle Innovation (FSLCI), with the objective of integrating potential environmental impacts of marine litter, especially plastic, into LCA results. This effort aims to provide a more comprehensive picture of potential environmental impacts and to support the identification of trade-offs associated with the use of plastic and other materials in product systems.
Because these CFs may not yet be readily available or fully operationalized in commonly used LCA software and LCI databases, practitioners may need to perform complementary calculations outside their usual modelling workflow. Depending on the software, database, and modelling approach used, this may concern the preparation of the LCI, the application of CFs during LCIA, or both.
Using this guide should therefore enable practitioners with different levels of experience to consistently integrate contributions from physical effects on biota into their LCAs, either at midpoint or damage level, while making transparent the assumptions, data choices, and calculation steps required for implementation.

title: Assessing Plastic Impacts in Life Cycle Assessment: A Practitioner’s Guide
text:
Content
This guide comprises seven main sections, including this introductory section.

Section 1 presents the rationale underpinning the development of the CFs, retraces their methodological development within the MarILCA framework, and explains what aspects of environmental impact they are intended to characterize. It situates the work within its broader methodological context and outlines both achieved milestones and ongoing developments.
Section 2 provides guidance on when physical effects on biota from plastic litter emissions should be accounted for in LCA studies. It discusses the practical implications of the current disconnect between available CFs and the limited representation of plastic litter flows in LCI databases. It then introduces screening questions to help practitioners determine whether further assessment is relevant, proportionate, and feasible.
Section 3 provides detailed step-by-step guidance for integrating the CFs into LCAs, covering the LCI, LCIA, and interpretation phases. Particular attention is given to key practical challenges, including the identification and selection of relevant inventory flows, the consistent application of CFs during impact assessment, and the robust interpretation of results.
Section 4 presents the main data sources currently available to support the quantification of plastic emissions in LCA studies. It reviews recent initiatives, including the Plastic Leak Project and the Plastic Footprint Network, that have contributed to the development of emission factors for activities and sectors prone to plastic leakage. The section also summarizes the current coverage of available data, highlights remaining gaps across sectors and emission pathways, and directs practitioners to relevant sources of information for estimating plastic emission flows within the scope of their assessments.
Section 5 presents fully developed case studies from selected industrial sectors, illustrating how the methodology is applied step by step and supporting correct implementation of the CFs.
Section 6 Addresses recurring questions, frequently encountered issues, and methodological uncertainties. Users are encouraged to consult this section when encountering practical or conceptual challenges during their assessments.

title: 1  Background
text:
1.1 Plastics: functional benefits and environmental concerns
Plastics have become deeply embedded in modern economies due to their versatility, low density, durability, barrier properties, and relatively low production costs. These properties make them useful across a wide range of applications, including packaging, healthcare, construction, transportation, and electronics. In some systems, plastics can contribute to material efficiency, product protection, reduced transport burdens, or longer service life. These benefits should be acknowledged, because the environmental relevance of plastic products depends on the function delivered and on the full life cycle considered. Reflecting their widespread use, cumulative primary plastic production was estimated to have reached approximately 9.5 billion tonnes by 2019 (Geyer et al. 2017), and annual production continues to increase (Figure 1.1).
At the same time, the scale of plastic production and use has resulted in growing plastic stocks within the technosphere and increasing waste flows requiring end-of-life management. Yet only a limited fraction of plastic waste is successfully recycled globally, commonly estimated at 9.3% (Figure 1.2). As a result, substantial quantities of plastic waste are landfilled, incinerated, mismanaged, or released to natural environments. In an LCA context, the key issue is therefore not only the generation of plastic waste, but the fraction of plastic flows that may leave the technosphere and become plastic emissions to environmental compartments.
Global assessments provide an indication of both the scale and the sources of plastic leakage to the environment. OECD estimates suggest that around 22 Mt of plastics entered natural environments in 2019, reflecting the combined effects of high plastic consumption and insufficient waste management systems (Figure 1.3). Most of these emissions were macroplastics (MAP), representing approximately 19.4 Mt, primarily associated with inadequate waste collection and disposal practices. Additional contributions arose from littering, and marine-based activities. Although smaller in quantity, microplastics (MIP, typically defined as particles ranging from 1 µm to 5 mm) represented a significant fraction of total leakage and were mainly generated through dust, tyre abrasion, wastewater sludge, and losses of industrial plastic pellets (OECD 2022).
Once released into terrestrial, freshwater, or marine ecosystems, plastics can generate significant ecological impacts (Figure 1.4). Larger plastic debris, termed macroplastics (MAP), can be ingested by fauna or cause entanglement, leading to injury, impaired mobility, reduced feeding capacity, or mortality in birds, mammals, fish, reptiles or other taxa (Beaumont et al. 2019). Beyond these visible impacts, fragmentation processes driven by UV radiation, mechanical abrasion, and biological activity progressively generate smaller particles. These microplastics and nanoplastics (<1 µm) may either be intentionally produced at small sizes (primary microplastics) or result from the breakdown of larger items (secondary microplastics).
As particle size decreases, the spectrum of potentially exposed organisms broadens. Micro- (MIP) and nanoplastics can be ingested by a wide range of species, including zooplankton, benthic invertebrates, and other organisms at the base of trophic networks. In aquatic environments, exposure may occur through feeding, filtration, or ventilation processes (Wright et al. 2013; Besseling et al. 2015). Experimental evidence also indicates that micro- and nanoplastics can affect photoautotrophic organisms, including through effects on growth, photosynthetic activity, and oxidative stress, although responses vary depending on particle size, shape, polymer type, concentration, and exposure conditions (Zhang et al. 2017; Bhattacharya et al. 2010; Sjollema et al. 2016). Because these organisms contribute to primary production, nutrient cycling, and trophic transfer, effects at lower trophic levels may propagate through food webs and affect ecosystem functioning (Galloway et al. 2017; De Sá et al. 2018).
Given the scale of plastic production, the persistence of materials in the environment, and the diversity of exposure pathways and affected taxa, these impacts must be systematically considered when evaluating the environmental performance of products and services. Integrating Ecosystem Quality indicators related to plastic and microplastic emissions in LCA is therefore essential to ensure a more comprehensive and ecologically meaningful sustainability assessment.

text:
1.2 History of the plastic litter issue in LCA

1.2.1 Inventory data developments
The Plastic Leak Project (Peano et al. 2020) was the first science-based initiative aiming at developing inventory models allowing the quantification of plastic emissions towards the environment from various processes and activities. Their Sectorial Guidance Generic data allowed for the quantification of MIP or MAP leakage associated with four main processes (Peano et al. 2020):

Pellet production (MIPs),
Tire abrasion during transport (MIPs),
Microfibers releases from textile washing (MIPs), and
Losses occurring at the end-of-life through waste mismanagement or littering (MAPs) .

Building on this initiative, the Plastic Footprint Network (PFN) was launched in 2023 with a broader scope. While the Plastic Leak Project focused primarily on inventory models for quantifying plastic emissions, the PFN seek to connect plastic emissions inventories with impact assessment within a single cohesive framework. For the impact assessment step, the PFN relies on MarILCA and therefore mainly focuses its efforts on the development of the inventory step. In this regard, several PFN technical modules have been developed to address key sources of plastic leakage across the life cycle, including packaging, textiles, and textiles fibers, tires, fishing, fishing gear, agricultural plastics, and leakage associated with waste exports.
Other assessments provide overviews of global emissions without aiming to allocate or scale these emissions to specific product systems or activities (Cottom et al. 2024; Han et al. 2026). Such studies are useful for identifying major sources and pathways of plastic leakage on a global scale, but they do not provide the activity-based emission factors or modelling structure required for assessments at the product or service scale.


1.2.2 Available CFs for LCIA

1.2.2.1 Physical effects on biota (microplastics)
The following overview focuses on the development of CFs representing physical effects on biota within the MarILCA framework. MarILCA currently provides one of the most operational approaches in LCIA for quantifying potential impacts associated with MIP emissions to the environment.
The development of these CFs responded to a major gap in standard LCA practice. Before the launch of the MarILCA working group, plastic leakage from product systems, and the environmental consequences associated with such emissions, were generally not accounted for. Commonly used inventories did not include dedicated flows for identifying and quantifying plastic releases to environmental compartments, while LCIA methods did not provide CFs to characterize their potential impacts. This gap was explicitly highlighted by the Medellin Declaration on Marine Litter in Life Cycle Assessment and Management, which called for the integration of plastic litter issues into both inventory modelling and impact assessment (Sonnemann and Valdivia 2017). It was subsequently addressed through the creation of the MarILCA working group in 2018.
Within this context, a first major milestone was the development of a structured methodological framework to assess the potential impacts of plastic litter emissions (Figure 1.6). Woods et al. (2021) formalized this framework and established a clear research agenda, identifying the key modelling components required to derive CFs. With this conceptual foundation in place, subsequent work focused on progressively operationalizing the different building blocks needed to quantify physical effects on biota.






Figure 1.6: Project framework and projects



The operationalization of this framework began in 2022, the first of these building blocks was published, introducing a generic effect factor to account for physical effects on biota (Lavoie et al. 2022). Building on this contribution, Corella-Puertas et al. (2022) proposed an initial set of simplified CFs to estimate potential impacts on Ecosystem Quality resulting from emissions of expanded polystyrene and tire and road wear particles in aquatic environments. At that stage, the fate model was deliberately simplified, considering only degradation and sedimentation processes and relying on uncertain slow-to-fast degradation rates. Further methodological refinements followed, extending the framework to additional polymers and particle shapes. These developments culminated in the first official release of CFs in Corella-Puertas et al. (2023), which presented revised fate and effect factors.
Building on the 2023 release, subsequent developments broadened the model scope and improved its robustness. Saadi et al. (2025) incorporated impacts occurring in sediments, which had previously been omitted. This refinement led to substantial increases in CF values, particularly for high-density polymers whose longer residence times in sediments, combined with slow degradation processes, amplify potential impacts (Saadi et al. 2025). The same work also introduced CFs for semi-synthetic and cellulosic-based natural fibers. In early 2026, another significant update aligned the fate modelling approach with the USEtox consensus framework for toxicity and ecotoxicity impact categories (Rosenbaum et al. 2008; Fantke et al. 2021), integrating the work of Quik et al. (2024). At that stage, the revised model was applicable to spherical MIPs only. Finally, in late 2026, a consolidated and comprehensive version of the CFs was released, extending coverage to the three particle shapes identified in earlier stages of the research, namely spheres, fibers, and films, while also expanding the range of polymers and materials considered (Saadi et al., submitted).
Taken together, these CFs aim to quantitatively represent the potential detrimental physical effects of MIP emissions to natural environments on biodiversity, expressed under the area of protection Ecosystem Quality. A central feature of the framework is the explicit consideration of residence time across environmental compartments, which captures how transport, degradation, sedimentation, and accumulation influence the duration and magnitude of potential impact. Although CFs are provided in different units depending on their alignment with specific LCIA methodologies, the underlying objective remains consistent: to capture, in an operational and scientifically grounded manner, the potential physical effects of MIPs on biota. Despite these advances, important uncertainties remain, particularly regarding degradation dynamics, species sensitivity data, and the scaling of organism-level effects to biodiversity damage metrics.


1.2.2.2 Entanglement impacts from fishing gear (MAPs)
Spatially explicit CFs to quantify potential impacts on Ecosystem Quality from entanglement-prone MAP debris, particularly lost fishing gear, have recently been developed by Høiberg et al. (2024). These CFs are provided at the scale of exclusive economic zones (EEZs) and as country-level averages, representing a significant advancement in the spatial differentiation of MAP impacts. However, their methodological framework is not fully aligned with the modelling approach used in MarILCA for MIP emissions, which limits their direct integration within a unified impact assessment framework.
First, the fate modelling underlying Høiberg et al. (2024) does not explicitly quantify the residence time of debris across environmental compartments in a manner consistent with multimedia fate modelling approaches typically applied in LCIA. The period during which debris may remain available to entangle organisms must therefore be assessed separately, which can be particularly challenging for non-experts. As a result, temporal dynamics are not treated in a way that is directly comparable to MIP fate modelling in Corella-Puertas et al. (2023), Saadi et al. (2025), or Louvet et al. (2026). Second, the effect modelling does not rely on endpoints such as mortality, impaired reproduction, or reduced growth, which are more directly aligned with the consensus toxicity framework used in USEtox (Rosenbaum et al. 2008). Instead, the approach estimates the fraction of potentially affected species based on their susceptibility to interacting with entanglement-prone MAP debris. This may lead to conservative estimates of potential impact, since not all interactions necessarily translate into ecologically relevant damage at the population level.
Finally, the scope of the CFs developed by Høiberg et al. (2024) is restricted to debris with entanglement-prone geometries, such as fishing nets and lines. This limits their applicability to a specific subset of MAP items and makes it difficult to systematically link these CFs to the diverse range of product shapes encountered in product-level LCAs. Consequently, while these CFs represent a valuable step toward integrating MAP entanglement impacts into LCIA, further methodological harmonisation would be required to ensure consistency with MIP impact pathways.
Despite these limitations, these CFs have been tested in combination with CFs for physical effects on biota from MIP emissions in a fishing industry case study. The results showed that MAP entanglement impacts can be highly relevant for Ecosystem Quality, particularly for anchoveta fishing, where they dominated the results under the assumptions tested. For cod fishing, entanglement was also an important contributor, although it was not necessarily the dominant one when other impact categories were included. The results were highly sensitive to the assumed time horizon over which debris remained capable of causing entanglement impacts, which remains a major source of uncertainty.



1.2.3 Additive coverage in LCA
While CFs representing the environmental impacts of plastic emissions have been developed and continue to evolve, most available developments focus on physical impacts and therefore exclude chemical impacts associated with the specific composition of products (Woods et al. 2021; Lavoie et al. 2022; Corella-Puertas et al. 2023; Saadi et al. 2025; Louvet et al. 2026). Everyday plastic products can contain non-negligible amounts of chemical additives used to modify or enhance product properties, including plasticizers, flame retardants, pigments, antistatic agents, biocides, and light stabilizers (Vincoff et al. 2024; Monclús et al. 2025). This issue has been recognized within the MarILCA framework but is not addressed by the CFs introduced in the previous section. The physical effects on biota pathway characterizes plastic particles through their polymer fraction and does not account for formulation-specific additives. By contrast, chemical effects associated with additives would need to be represented through ecotoxicity-related modelling, provided that the identity, amount, release, fate, and toxicity of the relevant substances can be specified (Woods et al. 2021; Lavoie et al. 2022; Corella-Puertas et al. 2023). However, as reported by Logan et al. (2024), additive coverage in LCI databases remains highly limited, partly because exact formulations are often unavailable due to industrial confidentiality and competitiveness concerns Law et al. (2024).
Current assessments suggest that most potential impacts on Ecosystem Quality attributable to plastic emissions are associated with the polymer fraction rather than with additive substances leaching from plastic items (Lavoie et al., 202X). These results indicate that the main contributors to Ecosystem Quality impacts may already be captured by the physical effects on biota CFs. However, when CFs are applied to the total mass of a plastic item rather than only to its polymer fraction, impacts may be slightly overestimated because additives are implicitly treated as part of the characterized polymer mass, for which the CFs are greater than additives. In practice, however, information on the additive composition of plastic items remains too sparse to support precise and systematic impact assessment with the current state of knowledge.


1.2.4 Work in progress CFs for LCIA

1.2.4.1 Human toxicity non-cancer (MIP)
MIP emissions to natural environments have the potential to generate impacts on human health through both the inhalation of airborne MIPs and the ingestion of contaminated food and beverages (Lamichhane et al. 2023; Azoulay et al. 2019). Indeed, plants and animals consumed by humans, such as rice, fish, and seafood have been shown to contain non-negligible amounts of MIPs (Dessì et al., 2021; Ribeiro et al., 2020; Anastasopoulou et al., 2018). MIPs have also been detected in multiple human tissues, demonstrating that they can enter the human body, bypass protective barriers, and potentially lead to deleterious health effects (Koelmans et al. 2022; Magana-Arachchi and Wanigatunge 2023).
The impact pathway currently under development considers the distribution of MIPs in the environment after emission, as well as their bioconcentration and bioaccumulation in food. Human exposure, based on region-average diets, is then combined with non-cancer toxicological effects derived from mammalian data, thereby providing a first set of CFs, which are expected to be available in late 2026.


1.2.4.2 Marine carbon pump (MIP)
This model is currently under development, and the first CFs should be available in 2027.


1.2.4.3 Ingestion of micro- and macroplastics
New developments have also been proposed for combined MIP and MAP ingestion. Indeed, Marhoon et al. (2026) addressed another physical impact pathway associated with plastic emissions: ingestion by marine species, which had already been partially considered in previous work for MIP. The authors developed a global EF to quantify the fraction of marine air-breathing vertebrate species potentially affected by macro- and microplastic ingestion. The model covers marine mammals, seabirds, and sea turtles, and is based on field observations of plastic ingestion prevalence in stranded and bycaught individuals across several ocean basins. Species-specific exposure was estimated using spatially explicit plastic concentration data for floating debris at the ocean surface, combined with species range information. These data were then used to derive dose-response relationships and construct a field-based SSD (species sensitivity distribution).
The resulting EF is expressed in PAF·km³/kg and represents the increase in the fraction of potentially affected species per unit increase in plastic concentration in marine surface water. Marhoon et al. (2026) estimated an HC20EC10 of 51.7 kg/km³, corresponding to an EF of 3.87 × 10⁻³ PAF·km³/kg. This value is approximately three orders of magnitude higher than the EF used for MIP physical effects on biota in Corella-Puertas et al. (2023), which was subsequently applied or further developed in later CF developments such as Saadi et al. (2025) and Louvet et al. (2026). This difference partly reflects the broader scope of the ingestion EF, which covers both macro- and microplastics and is derived from field-based ingestion prevalence data, whereas earlier MIP effect modelling is based on laboratory-derived evidence and combines several physical effect mechanisms rather than treating ingestion as a distinct pathway.
This development is important because it provides a first operational basis for representing plastic ingestion as a specific physical impact pathway in LCIA, including for MAP, for which ingestion impacts had previously not been characterized. However, the EF should be interpreted as an intermediate and generic estimate. It does not quantify observed biological damage following ingestion, but instead assumes that ingestion may lead to lethal or sub-lethal physical effects. It is also generic with respect to polymer type, particle shape, and plastic size, and currently focuses only on marine air-breathing vertebrates exposed to floating debris. Marhoon et al. therefore recommend coupling this EF with appropriate fate modelling before full integration into LCIA, following the broader framework proposed for plastic litter impact assessment.

1.3 Future directions for CF development

1.3.1 Additional disruptions of the carbon cycle
MIP emissions to natural environments have been shown to interfere with carbon cycling through multiple mechanisms, extending beyond the biological carbon pump disruption. In particular, adverse effects on phytoplankton, zooplankton, and soil biota communities may alter primary production, trophic interactions, microbial respiration processes, and organic carbon turnover, thereby affecting carbon sequestration (Zhu et al. 2025). Such ecological perturbations could translate into measurable shifts in both marine and terrestrial carbon dynamics, although their magnitude and direction remain context-dependent and insufficiently quantified for operational integration into LCIA.
Zhu et al. (2025) further identify additional mechanisms that may appear secondary when considered individually, but could cumulatively contribute to broader changes in carbon dynamics. Despite their potential relevance at larger spatial and temporal scales, these pathways are not currently represented in LCIA models. Their integration would require dedicated fate, exposure, and effect modelling frameworks, together with corresponding CFs. Progress in this direction will depend on the availability of sufficiently robust empirical datasets to support quantitative relationships between MIP exposure, ecological responses, and carbon cycle feedbacks.

title: 2  When should physical effects on biota be accounted for?
text:
Accounting for the physical effects of plastic litter on biota requires additional attention at both the LCI and LCIA stages. Although some LCIA methods, such as IMPACT World+ v2.1, now include CFs for physical effects on biota, the corresponding elementary flows for plastic litter emissions are generally not available or are not systematically populated in commonly used LCI databases. Consequently, even when practitioners use an LCIA method that includes these CFs, plastic emissions often need to be quantified separately before they can be characterized.
In practice, this means that foreground data may need to be complemented with specific estimates of plastic leakage, while background datasets may not systematically include plastic emissions. Depending on the case study, practitioners may therefore need to perform additional calculations to estimate inventory flows, apply the CFs, or both. This additional work can be valuable, but it may not be necessary or proportionate for all assessments.
Users should therefore consider the following screening questions before proceeding with a full assessment of contributions from plastic litter emissions.
Questions to guide the decision on including physical effects on biota in impact assessment studies






NoteClient and commissioner intent






Has the client explicitly required the assessment of the environmental consequences of plastic litter within the study scope?
Is the client particularly concerned with plastic litter as an environmental issue, whether for reputational, regulatory, or advocacy reasons?
Are the study results intended for public disclosure or to support a comparative assertion, where omitting plastic litter impacts could be challenged or scrutinized?
Is the study conducted within a regulatory or sectoral framework that mandates the reporting of plastic litter impacts?
In your professional judgment, would omitting plastic litter impacts from this study scope constitute a material failure to adequately address the stated goal and intended application of the study, in a way that could not be justified on scientific or methodological grounds?










NoteGoal and scope relevance






Does the stated goal of the study include Ecosystem Quality or biodiversity among the relevant areas of protection?
Does the product system involve plastic materials that could plausibly be released as litter into the environment, as opposed to being used exclusively in industrial, closed-loop, or fully controlled-waste contexts?
Is this a comparative study in which one or more alternatives are predominantly made of plastic while others are not, such that plastic litter impacts could be a differentiating factor between systems?










NoteMateriality






Does the product system contain a significant mass fraction of plastics relative to other materials?
Do the plastics involved belong to categories with inherently high litter probability, such as single-use items, flexible food packaging, agricultural films, or fishing gear?
Is the geographic context of use or disposal associated with insufficient waste-management infrastructure, leading to substantially higher environmental litter release rates?
Has a preliminary screening or hotspot analysis indicated that plastic litter flows are non-negligible relative to other inventory flows or impact categories in the system?










NoteForeground Actionability






Are the plastic litter flows that are likely to be significant located in the foreground system, where the practitioner can realistically model the emissions?
In a comparative study, do the foreground systems of the compared alternatives differ meaningfully in their plastic litter emission profiles, or are these contributions roughly equivalent across alternatives?










NoteFeasibility






Is reliable data available, whether primary or from well-documented secondary sources, to quantify plastic litter emission factors for the specific product categories, use contexts, and geographies covered by the study?
Does the practitioner have sufficient expertise in plastic litter impact modeling, or a clear willingness to acquire it, to carry out the additional assessment steps with adequate rigor?
Are the study timeline and budget sufficient to accommodate the additional data collection, modeling, and reporting effort required?

3.2 Life cycle inventory for the foreground system

3.2.1 Processes and materials
As a first step in your assessment, the processes in which emissions of plastic pieces or particles can occur must be identified. Here, the focus should be on the foreground system, for reasons mentioned in the previous sections. The processes typically associated with plastic leakage are likely to be similar to the modules identified in the PFN or the PLP. For all types of plastic products, emissions are indeed likely to occur during plastic granulate manufacturing, road transportation with tire abrasion and end-of-life management, including littering. Some processes also concern specific sectors. This applies, for example, to the washing of garments and textiles during the use stage, where microfibers are emitted to wastewater. The same reasoning applies to the fishing industry, which can lose fishing gear at sea, and agricultural practices involving mulch films.
For end-of-life processes, it is also important to highlight that leakage could occur via multiple pathways. Littered, uncollected and improperly disposed waste may all end up in natural environments but differ greatly in proportions. Also, waste can be suboptimally managed without necessarily leaking totally to the environment. This distinction is relevant and justifies the need for a precise identification of processes involved in the targeted systems during the assessment. Some plastic emissions can also originate from waste exports. Indeed, waste mismanagement that occurs once exported waste lands in a country with inefficient waste management infrastructure also could be taken into consideration. This is the case for many high-income countries that export a significant fraction of their plastic waste to low or middle-income countries that rely on poor waste management schemes.
The identification of the processes involved in the plastic emissions should allow practitioners to also identify the polymer composition of the emissions, which constitutes relevant information since CFs for physical effects on biota are available per polymer (e.g. PET, HDPE and PP) or material (e.g. cotton and viscose). This composition of emissions is directly related to the composition of the materials assessed. Therefore, when conducting the environmental assessment of a PET food container, for example, the emissions will be constituted of PET.

3.2.2 Geographical location
The geographic location of emission is a key parameter, as the physical fate and effects of MIP on biota are regionalized. CFs are therefore available for the following regions: Africa & Middle East, Central Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America, Northern Regions, Oceania, Southeast Asia, and a default World region (Table 3.2 provides a full listing of available regions). Regional differentiation accounts for parameters such as rainfall rate, water body depth and area, species richness, area fraction, and runoff, all of which influence the environmental fate and ultimate impact of MIP.
Practitioners should therefore identify the geographic region in which the processes and activities under study occur, as this determines which regional CF values to apply. For instance, road transport activities taking place during distribution stages in North America should be characterized using the North America CF values. The same logic applies to manufacturing processes, which may represent another source of MIP emissions and can occur across multiple regions within a single product system. When the location of emission cannot be determined, the World region should be used as the default.

3.2.3 Quantities
Following the identification of processes involved in plastic emissions throughout the life cycle of the product system under study, the quantification of these processes must be undertaken. The data used for this purpose may be labelled as emission factors, loss rates, leakage rates, or release rates, and communicate the quantity of plastic (expressed as mass) emitted by a process per unit of activity or per unit of material, for example. Note that mass is currently the designated metric of interest for quantifying plastic emissions. Particle count is also recognized as an important metric in MIP science, particularly for toxicity assessment (Thornton Hampton et al. 2022); however, mass remains the only unit used in the LCA field to date. Accordingly, any data expressed in particle numbers must be converted to mass using information on particle size and density before use in an LCA context. Lavoie et al. (2022) and Besseling et al. (2019) provide worked examples of such conversions.
Various conventions are used throughout the scientific and industrial literature to express quantities of emitted plastics. Emission factors are frequently expressed as percentages or fractions, representing the proportion of a plastic material considered to be emitted to the environment, but may also be expressed as a mass of plastic per unit of process or activity. Some of the variation observed in units and terminology is attributable to differences in what is being quantified. For instance, in the dataset published by the Plastic Footprint Network (PFN; Plastic Footprint Guidelines (2023)), loss rates quantify direct emissions, whereas release rates quantify emissions reaching specific environmental compartments following release and subsequent redistribution; whether through natural processes (e.g., transport of MIP from freshwater to oceans via currents) or human interventions (e.g., wastewater treatment). It is therefore essential for practitioners to carefully examine what each data source is expressing and quantifying before use.

A related and critical issue concerns the risk of double-counting fate when estimating quantities of plastic emissions to natural environments. 3.2.4 Environmental compartment
CFs for MIP are compartment-dependent and are available for the following emission compartments: air, agricultural soil, lake water, natural soil, river water, and sea water (see Table 3.6). In practice, the receiving compartment may be straightforward to identify for some processes but difficult to determine precisely for others.
Precise compartment assignment requires detailed information on where plastic emissions occur and, where relevant, how leaked plastic is transported before reaching the receiving environment. This level of detail is often unavailable to practitioners. Ideally, activity-specific leakage models would provide this information in the same way that LCI datasets provide elementary flows for a wide range of substances and activities. However, plastic emissions are not yet systematically represented in these data sources. For now, practitioners therefore need to rely on complementary data sources and transparent assumptions.
At the time of writing, the most useful source of information on this matter is the PFN technical modules and accompanying spreadsheets. These include partial pre-fate allocation through release rates, which indicate the share of leaked plastic assigned to different receiving compartments. In the PFN data sheets used for this guide, the granularity and completeness of release rates vary by sector.
For example, in the Macroplastic: Packaging spreadsheet, the “Leaked to Ocean and Waterways” column provides country-specific release rates for a combined marine and freshwater compartment. This helps estimate releases to aquatic environments but does not distinguish between sea water, river water, and lake water, and therefore does not allow direct selection of the most specific CF. The same spreadsheet provides additional generic release rates for ocean and land, depending on the size of the emitted plastic item and its residual value. Larger items and items with higher residual value are associated with lower release rates. These release rates may not sum to 100%, because the remaining fraction is assumed to be removed, for example, through waste picking or municipal cleaning operations.
As a pragmatic default, we recommend first using the mismanaged fraction per country and then applying the generic release rates for ocean and land from the lower table to allocate the emitted fraction between continental sea water and continental natural soil, respectively. Alternatively, practitioners may assume that the “Leaked to Ocean and Waterways” fraction is emitted to sea water and that the remaining emitted fraction is released to land, represented here as natural soil. This simplified allocation should be documented, and fractions assumed to be removed or cleaned should not be characterized as emissions.
For MIP emissions from textile production and use, emissions to land should be assigned to agricultural soil, since the release pathway occurs via sewage sludge spreading on agricultural fields. Recommendations on compartment assignment are provided in Table 3.6.
For MIP emissions from tire abrasion, we strongly recommend using the specific CFs available in Saadi and Boulay (2026) where applicable, as these incorporate a weighting based on the likelihood of emissions reaching different natural compartments at the continental scale. Further parameterization is possible using PFN data to adapt the emission distribution according to watershed size and the share of driving occurring in rural, urban, and highway contexts. Because updates to the PFN methodology and data are expected, these recommendations should be revisited when new versions become available.

3.2.5 Fragmentation
For many of the emitting processes identified previously, the plastic emissions will take the form of MAPs. Yet CFs for physical effects on biota are only available for micro-sized plastic emissions. Secondary plastics, which originate from microplastic fragmentation, are nevertheless thought to be the most abundant form of microplastics, more so than primary microplastics manufactured as such (Mutuku et al. 2024). This means that MAPs undergo significant fragmentation under the forces encountered in the environment. It is therefore generally accepted that a significant proportion of the MAPs that end up in natural environments will fragment over time, especially over long time horizons.
On this matter, a few recommendations can be put forward, based on a peer-reviewed degradation and fragmentation model (Tang et al., submitted). The idea is simply to use a percentage value (%) to represent the proportion of MAP emissions that will fragment and should thus be characterized using the CFs for physical effects on biota. These fragmentation percentages vary by material type (i.e. rigid or flexible) and emission compartment (i.e. topsoil, beach, or water surface). The rationale is that a flexible material likely has a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio than a rigid polymer, making it more susceptible to fragmentation. As for emission compartments, UV intensity and mechanical forces influence the fragmentation observed, and thus the variable rates across compartments. 3.2.7 Size
CFs expressing damage to biodiversity from MIP emissions span up to 6 orders of magnitude across the 1–5000 µm size range. Particle size is therefore a critical parameter in LCA assessments, as the choice of size class can significantly influence results. For primary MIP; particles manufactured and released directly at the micro scale; size characterization is generally straightforward, as their dimensions are defined at the point of production and should be known to the practitioner.
Fragmentation breaks larger plastic pieces into smaller debris, which can eventually become part of what is referred to as micro- or nano-plastics (< 5 mm). The size distribution of microplastics after fragmentation from macro-sized litter is deeply uncertain. Because CFs can vary by up to 6 orders of magnitude depending on emitted particle size (Louvet et al. 2026), this information is crucial for precisely and rigorously assessing the potential damages on biodiversity caused by emissions of plastic litter in natural environments.
In this context, several avenues may shed light on the matter. Based on the commonness of microplastic sizes found in the environment and in industry, Corella-Puertas et al. (2023) proposes default sizes for the various shapes of microplastics. For generic plastic materials (MAPs) (e.g. buoys, kettles, and toys) that must be characterized as microplastics in order to use the physical effects on biota CFs, the recommended size class is 1000 µm or 5000 µm, since large particles will likely dominate the fragmented mass during the early stages of fragmentation (Egger et al. 2020); Kaandorp et al. 3.2.8 Limits of the inventory of plastic emissions
Limits and weaknesses of plastic emission inventories exist and are worth highlighting, since they can significantly influence the results of the assessment. Because CFs for physical effects on biota are quite large, especially for large particle sizes and high-density polymers, a small variation in the quantities of emitted plastics can shift the conclusions of a study.
Drawing on experience from previous work estimating plastic emissions to natural environments, the most pressing limit of the inventory concerns the fragmentation of MAPs into secondary microplastics, which can then be characterized using the physical effects on biota CFs. The wide range of assumptions made on this question in the past; 10%, 50%, and 100% (Corella-Puertas et al. 2023; Plastic Footprint Guidelines 2023); 0.5% (Erradhouani et al. 2026); 100% (Louvet et al. 2026); and 4%, 12%, and 62% (Saadi et al. 2025); reveals the substantial unknowns associated with this parameter, especially given the variety of product types, environmental conditions, and polymer chemistries involved. We therefore recommend always including a sensitivity analysis on the value of this parameter.
A further limitation concerns the focus on the foreground system. Since plastic emission inventories are not currently assessed in LCI databases, background systems will essentially never include plastic emissions, even though in reality many occur in background packaging and oceanic freight activities, for example.
Most limits faced during the inventory stage will likely originate from data availability. Some sectors may be unable to find accurate and reliable data on the plastic emissions occurring throughout their supply chain. Because data may come from many sources, methodologies and assumptions may also differ, inducing considerable uncertainty in the assessment. Furthermore, obtaining uncertainty estimates (e.g. confidence intervals) for inventory emission factors is mostly impossible given the current state of knowledge in the field.
Specific limitations are also linked to particular data sources or methodologies. For example, in low-income countries (LICs) and middle-income countries (MICs), open dumps are the de facto treatment for waste disposal. Yet some methodologies, such as the PFN (Plastic Footprint Guidelines 2023) and the PLP (Peano et al. 2020), consider this end-of-life treatment as waste mismanagement and apply a 100% leakage to litter taking this path. While there is consensus that open dumps are far from optimal, this approach stands in stark contrast to other scientific studies, which instead suggest leakage rates of 0.04% (Cottom et al. 2024), 5% (Schwarz et al. 2023), and 25% (OECD 2022). These values, although widely scattered, all differ significantly from the 100% assumed by the PLP (Peano et al. 2020) and the PFN (Plastic Footprint Guidelines 2023).
Similarly, potential plastic emissions resulting from plastic waste exports are not currently accounted for directly by the emission factors provided in the PFN (Plastic Footprint Guidelines 2023). The share of plastic waste exported is provided, but linking these exports to specific destination countries and assigning the corresponding emission factors of waste treated there requires additional data and work by the practitioner. Quantifying emissions from plastic waste exports is nonetheless possible. To do so, practitioners can rely on the waste-export shares given in the PFN data for the country where the end-of-life of their product system occurs. Identifying the destination countries would be ideal; alternatively, practitioners may use the average waste-mismanagement percentages for low- and middle-income countries provided in the PLP data, and multiply the two values to estimate the resulting emission factors. The usual release step is then followed as normal to identify the natural compartments where emissions occur.
The limited transparency of data provided by some initiatives makes it difficult to modify emission factors to reflect the specific context of a study, or to integrate partial data the practitioner may already have; ultimately limiting their control over the quality and representativeness of their assessment.
On the operational side, practitioners may also face practical limitations in the time needed to account for contributions from physical effects on biota. Since the process described in the previous sections is not yet fully integrated into databases and software the way other impact categories are, additional steps are necessary to incorporate these contributions into the tables and figures communicating the results. This can prove particularly cumbersome when multiple products, scenarios, and sensitivity analyses are carried out over the course of the assessment.

3.3 Life cycle impact assessment (LCIA)

3.3.1 Physical effects on biota
The CFs for physical effects on biota express the potential detrimental impacts on species communities associated with emissions of MIP to natural environments. They account for both the potential effects of MIP on exposed organisms and the residence time of MIP in the environmental compartments through which particles may be transported. They are available on two time scales, representing short- and long-term time-horizon perspectives, similar to the Climate change short-term and long-term indicators available in the IMPACT World+ methodology. Following the same approach as Climate change, the short-term physical effects on biota CFs quantify the potential impacts occurring during the 0–100 year time horizon, while the long-term CFs quantify those occurring beyond 100 years.
As indicated by the name of the impact category, the current CFs account only for physical effects. This reflects the way the effect factors were developed: they rely on ecotoxicological data from experiments using virgin MIP, in order to isolate the physical effects of plastic particles on organisms, without including potential effects from additives or other chemicals present in plastic product matrices (Lavoie et al. 2022; Corella-Puertas et al. 2022, 2023; Saadi et al. 2025; Louvet et al. 2026; Saadi and Boulay 2026).
Chemical substances added to plastic products to modify or enhance their properties, such as additives, are therefore not represented in the physical effects on biota pathway. When relevant, and when sufficient inventory and substance-specific data are available, these chemical contributions should instead be considered through existing ecotoxicity impact pathways. Similarly, the fate modelling focuses on the intrinsic properties of the polymer particles; for example, degradation and fragmentation behaviour; and does not explicitly account for formulation-specific effects such as additional stability induced by additives. ?sec-physical-vs-ecotox discusses the distinction between physical effects on biota and ecotoxicity, and proposes approaches for addressing this issue in practice.
The physical effects considered in this pathway include entanglement, ingestion, and adherence. These mechanisms may lead to adverse outcomes such as mortality, reduced growth, reduced feeding, or reduced reproduction.
The CFs are provided for 14 materials, 5 sizes, 4 shapes, 9 environmental compartments, and 2 scales. These are listed in Table 3.18, and the CFs themselves are available here.

3.3.1.1 Units for various modeling frameworks and LCIA methodologies
Various methodologies are available to practitioners for the LCIA step of their assessment. These methodologies combine different models across a number of impact categories and sometimes also imply a series of value choices in their modeling assumptions (e.g. the time horizons considered). LCIA methods are generally either midpoint- or damage-oriented, though some cover both (Bulle et al. 2019). The physical effects on biota impact category provides CFs at both midpoint and damage levels and is implemented in IMPACT World+ (Bulle et al. 2019), one of the most widely used LCIA methodologies available. Additionally, to facilitate their integration with diverse LCIA methodologies, the physical effects on biota CFs are provided in different versions, using different units.


3.3.1.2 Limits of the model
Models are imperfect representations of real-world processes. The modeling involved in the development of the CFs is no exception and thus carries many limitations. One of the main limitations stems from data availability, especially for the polymer degradation rates used in developing the fate factors. Quality experiments are scarce, so obtaining enough data to accurately represent the various mechanisms and environmental stresses that govern degradation rates across the range of existing polymers is a significant challenge given current knowledge (tang2026?).

The approach is straightforward: the emitted quantities of MIP are multiplied by the appropriate CF, following the usual LCIA procedure. Each quantity is multiplied by the appropriate CF; at midpoint or damage level, depending on the practitioner’s needs; to obtain its contribution to the impact indicator. 3.3.2 Limits of the impact assessment of plastic emissions
Models are incomplete representations of reality and therefore carry numerous limitations. For the impact assessment of plastic emissions specifically, several can be identified. First, the physical effects on biota CFs are for now only available for MIP-sized plastic particles. Combined with the uncertainty surrounding environmental fragmentation processes and the absence of CFs for MAP, this means that significant fractions of the plastic litter emitted to the environment may go unaccounted for at the impact assessment step. This results in a systematic underestimation of impacts and creates a mass-balance inconsistency: the total mass of plastic recorded in the life cycle inventory is not fully characterized at the impact assessment level, as MAPs are effectively assigned a zero-impact weight by default.
Second, current model assumptions focus on the physical effects on biota, which, as the impact category name suggests, are limited to the physical effects on organisms. This implies that plastic pieces leaking to the environment are assumed to be composed of 100% polymer chains, rather than a mix of polymer and the chemical additives that complement the functionality of real plastic products on the market. This is a significant shortcoming, since it means the chemical toxicity of such substances; and of other components such as un-polymerized monomers; is currently unaccounted for. This may, however, matter less than it sounds for the impact assessment of plastic litter, because the relative mass of potential additives currently treated as polymer material may not be as harmful to ecosystems as is often assumed (Lavoie et al. 2022; Corella-Puertas et al. 2023; Louvet et al. 2026).
Third, regarding the modeling of the physical effects on biota, many limitations are reported in the papers describing the development of the model’s various components. They include, but are not limited to: (1) the use of a single generic effect factor to represent the physical effect of particles ranging from 0.001 µm to 5000 µm in all aquatic compartments, even though different sizes induce different levels of toxicity per kg of emissions (Thornton Hampton et al. 2022; Bobori et al. 2022) and impacts may vary with the species communities of different ecosystems; and (2) the lack of a consistent degradation model across all polymers and compartments, which can distort the residence time of MIP considered in the fate factors (Louvet et al. 2026).
Finally, it is crucial to remember that the cause-effect chains developed so far address only the potential damages on biodiversity (Ecosystem Quality area of protection) generated by ingestion, adherence, entanglement, and other physical effects. Yet it is widely acknowledged that plastic emissions also have detrimental consequences for human health (Human Health area of protection) and for resource availability and ecosystem services (Resources and Ecosystem Services area of protection) (Kumar et al. 2021; Gabisa et al. 2023). Further damages on biodiversity are also possible through interactions with other impact categories such as Climate change, as described in Section 1.2.4.2. The LCA community recognizes this, and the MarILCA framework identifies the development of cause-effect models linking plastic emissions to these endpoints as part of the work ahead (Woods et al. 2021). Other impact categories and areas of protection may therefore not reveal any impact contributions from plastic emissions for now, but these are simply hidden, rather than nonexistent.


3.3.3 Other considerations for the impact assessment of plastic products
In practice, the distinction between the two impact pathways, physical effects on biota and ecotoxicity, is also genuinely important. In most cases, practitioners may not have access to robust data on the additive composition of the plastic products under study, since this information is scarce and barely accessible. In such contexts, the recommendation is to consider the full mass of plastic as virgin (Approach A, Figure 3.2). This can be seen as a conservative approach, since the impact contributions from the polymer fraction greatly surpass those from additives (Lecointre et al. 2025). When information on additive content is available, separating the polymer and additive fractions and characterizing each independently, using the available CFs for physical effects on biota and ecotoxicity, respectively, is an improved yet still simple way of handling the issue (Approach B, Figure 3.2). This approach remains imperfect, as it assumes the effect, fate, and exposure of both fractions are independent once the plastic product is emitted to the environment, which is a significant assumption. It is also possible to assess the fate of additives in the polymer matrix more precisely, using tools such as the Food Contact Material tool in USEtox 3.0 (Approach C, Figure 3.2). This last approach offers a more robust and precise assessment of the fate of additives, but still carries shortcomings such as time constraints and data availability.

3.4 Interpretation

3.4.1 Analyzing the results (midpoint, damage)
Key differences in modeling assumptions exist between the physical effects on biota pathway and others, even closely related ones. For example, the treatment of substances that reach the global-scale marine compartment differs between the physical effects on biota model and the USEtox model, which addresses ecotoxicity impacts. The current USEtox 2.14 version treats pollutants as overwhelmingly diluted once they reach this global compartment, and therefore models their fate at the global scale as a removal mechanism from the environment. For MIP, the model was improved: the fate of MIP particles at the global scale is modeled in the same way as at the continental scale, so particles are considered to affect species at this scale too, even though the locations where concentrations can reach potentially toxic levels are extremely rare (in the case of physical effects on biota, outside the near-surface depths around marine gyres, where plastic litter tends to accumulate). This can lead to considerable variation in model outputs.
Similarly, the time horizons over which impacts are integrated can vary by impact category, which can distort the results; especially for damage-level indicators, which aggregate many inconsistent models into a single value. For example, the USEtox model, used as the consensus approach for the ecotoxicity and human toxicity impact categories, integrates potential impacts until a steady state is reached, which in practice means over an infinite time horizon. For Climate change, impacts are integrated over 100 years (short-term) or 500 years (long-term). These considerable differences generate significant discrepancies in output. Such limitations are present throughout LCIA methodologies and are not specific to the physical effects on biota framework.

Before the PFN (Earth Action 2023), which has been cited throughout the previous sections as a relevant data source, the PLP (Peano et al. 2020) was the first initiative to support the development of emission factors for activities prone to releasing of plastic particles into natural environments. At the time of writing, only three of the eight proposed modules have been completed and provide data: packaging covering macroplastics from waste mismanagement and littering; textiles, covering macroplastics from end-of-life mismanagement and microplastics from production and use-phase wastewater leakage; and tire abrasion, covering microplastics emissions. National statistics
Data on plastic emissions to the environment are also sometimes compiled by national agencies, with varying levels of granularity, often using material flow analysis (MFA) approaches. For example, Statistics Canada published the Physical Flow Account for Plastic Material in 2025 (Statistics Canada 2026)), which reports plastic flows and stocks from 2012 to 2021. Quantitative data on plastic leaked permanently to the environment are provided alongside other indicators, including total discarded plastic in products, the net stock of plastic in products remaining in use at the end of each year, and plastic products produced for Canadian consumption. These amounts are also reported for a range of product categories, from construction materials and electrical and electronic equipment to packaging, which is further subdivided into bottles, film, non-bottle rigid packaging and other packaging products. This type of data is particularly relevant for estimating emission factors associated with end-of-life management in Canada. Similar national or country-specific data sources may also be available for other contexts. For example, country-specific assessments have been carried out for Switzerland, providing detailed estimates of plastic flows and emissions that can support emission factor development (Kawecki and Nowack 2019; Jiang and Nowack 2025).
For information on the impact assessment models, useful data sources include, but are not limited to, the academic literature on the topic, especially the work of the MarILCA team and collaborators. These articles can support understanding of the meaning, scope, development approaches, and values of the CFs developed to date. Many of them also include case studies with transparent documentation of the assumptions and values used throughout the assessment, making them useful sources for inventory-related data as well.
